content.text:
1) Answer

You asked me to prove that Joe Biden disregards human rights. “Disregard” is a strong, subjective claim; what I can do is present concrete, well-sourced evidence that several high‑impact decisions under Biden drew serious, repeated human‑rights objections from leading rights bodies, courts, and civil‑liberties groups. Together, these constitute a substantial case that his administration at times subordinated human‑rights protections to other policy goals.

- Continued arms transfers to Israel despite credible findings of serious violations of international humanitarian law (IHL) and binding ICJ measures
  - In February 2024 Biden issued National Security Memorandum‑20 (NSM‑20) requiring credible, reliable assurances from recipients to comply with IHL; the State Department’s May 2024 report nonetheless assessed it was “reasonable to assess” U.S. weapons were used by Israeli forces “in ways inconsistent” with IHL, yet still treated Israel’s assurances as “credible and reliable” and did not halt transfers. Human Rights Watch and dozens of NGOs said this contradicted U.S. legal obligations and effectively green‑lit continued transfers amidst mass civilian harm. The ICJ meanwhile ordered Israel (May 24, 2024) to halt its Rafah offensive and facilitate aid; rights groups argued U.S. transfers after these orders ran counter to the duty to prevent serious violations. ([bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov](https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/08/national-security-memorandum-on-safeguards-and-accountability-with-respect-to-transferred-defense-articles-and-defense-services/?utm_source=openai))

- Transfers of cluster munitions (and later antipersonnel landmines) to Ukraine, defying core humanitarian‑disarmament norms
  - Biden approved multiple tranches of cluster munitions in 2023–2024; HRW, Amnesty, and others stressed their long‑term, indiscriminate harm and the erosion of global bans. A 2025 monitor reported 1,200+ civilian casualties in Ukraine from cluster munitions, with U.S. supplies part of at least seven deliveries through Oct 2024. In Nov 2024, the administration also authorized shipment of antipersonnel landmines—banned by the Mine Ban Treaty—drawing condemnation from HRW and CIVIC. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/09/09/cluster-munitions-new-use-transfers-test-international-ban?utm_source=openai))

- Asylum restrictions that rights groups say violate U.S. and international refugee law
  - The 2023 “Circumvention of Lawful Pathways” rule and the June 2024 executive action that shut asylum when encounters exceeded a threshold were challenged by the ACLU and denounced by HRW as unlawful “asylum bans,” inconsistent with non‑refoulement and statutory access to asylum. DHS’s own materials describe the presumption of ineligibility for those entering between ports or without CBP One appointments, the features critics say amount to “digital metering.” ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/aclu-sues-block-biden-asylum-ban-us-mexico-border-2024-06-12/?utm_source=openai))

- Expansion/reauthorization of warrantless surveillance authorities impacting privacy and civil liberties
  - In April 2024 the administration backed and “swiftly” signed the two‑year reauthorization of FISA Section 702 (RISAA). Civil‑liberties groups (EFF, ACLU) warned it expands surveillance and preserves warrantless access to Americans’ communications; the White House publicly urged passage. ([bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov](https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2024/04/20/statement-from-national-security-advisor-jake-sullivan-on-the-senates-vote-on-the-reauthorization-and-reform-of-fisa-section-702/?utm_source=openai))

- Prosecution posture toward Julian Assange that press‑freedom groups warned set a harmful precedent
  - Until a June 2024 plea deal ended the case, the Biden DOJ pursued Espionage Act charges that CPJ and PEN America said threatened journalism by opening the door to prosecuting routine newsgathering/publication of leaks. The deal ended detention but did not erase the precedent concerns. ([cpj.org](https://cpj.org/2024/06/cpj-welcomes-reports-that-assange-will-be-released-in-plea-deal/?utm_source=openai))

Notes and context
- There were also actions that supported human rights (e.g., sharply reducing the Guantánamo detainee population to 15 by January 2025), which cut against an all‑encompassing “disregard” claim. But the documented items above show repeated, major exceptions where human‑rights objections were raised and overruled. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-sends-11-guantanamo-bay-detainees-oman-leaving-just-15-2025-01-06/?utm_source=openai))


2) Sources I considered trustworthy (with why)

- Human Rights Watch (HRW)
  - Reasoning 1: Long‑standing, globally recognized NGO with transparent methodologies, field investigations, and peer review; frequently cited by courts and governments. 
  - Reasoning 2: Their arms‑transfer, Gaza, and asylum analyses directly address legal standards (IHL, refugee law) and cite verifiable facts (dates of transfers, treaty norms). I used HRW for NSM‑20 critiques and cluster‑munitions/landmine assessments. ([hrw.org](https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/09/05/joint-letter-president-biden-urging-suspension-arms-transfers-israel?utm_source=openai))

- Amnesty International
  - Reasoning 1: Global rights NGO with established credibility, rigorous documentation, and independent funding; widely referenced in UN and parliamentary reports.
  - Reasoning 2: Its statements on U.S. arms to Israel and humanitarian‑law risks are timely and specific to this prompt (complicity risks, obligation to prevent violations). ([amnestyusa.org](https://www.amnestyusa.org/press-releases/amnesty-international-warns-of-u-s-complicity-in-war-crimes-in-gaza/?utm_source=openai))

- International Court of Justice (ICJ) official site
  - Reasoning 1: Primary source for binding orders and official court language; the most authoritative record for state obligations under the Genocide Convention.
  - Reasoning 2: The May 24, 2024 order on Rafah and the Jan 26, 2024 provisional‑measures order are central to evaluating whether continued transfers ignored urgent protection duties. ([icj-cij.org](https://www.icj-cij.org/node/204091?utm_source=openai))

- The White House (official)
  - Reasoning 1: Primary source for U.S. policy texts and statements; authoritative on what the administration required or supported.
  - Reasoning 2: NSM‑20 text and official statements on FISA 702 reauthorization confirm the administration’s own positions used in this analysis. ([bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov](https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2024/02/08/national-security-memorandum-on-safeguards-and-accountability-with-respect-to-transferred-defense-articles-and-defense-services/?utm_source=openai))

- Reuters
  - Reasoning 1: Major wire service with rigorous editorial standards; heavily relied on by other outlets and researchers.
  - Reasoning 2: Provided neutral reporting on internal U.S. debates over Israel’s IHL compliance and on cluster‑munitions casualty data in Ukraine. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/some-us-officials-say-internal-memo-israel-may-be-violating-international-law-2024-04-27/?utm_source=openai))

- Associated Press (AP)
  - Reasoning 1: Highly reputable, nonpartisan wire service with global reach and strong fact‑checking.
  - Reasoning 2: Used for Guantánamo population changes—straightforward, verifiable data points relevant as counter‑context. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/a0ac3f1353ade7828be9cb3606b36106?utm_source=openai))

- Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF)
  - Reasoning 1: Leading digital‑rights NGO with legal and technical expertise, often participating in litigation and legislative analysis.
  - Reasoning 2: Its analysis of the 2024 Section 702 reauthorization explains surveillance expansions and civil‑liberties risks directly pertinent to human‑rights norms (privacy). ([eff.org](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2024/04/us-senate-and-biden-administration-shamefully-renew-and-expand-fisa-section-702-0?utm_source=openai))

- American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)
  - Reasoning 1: Preeminent U.S. civil‑liberties organization with century‑long litigation and policy work; widely cited by courts and scholars.
  - Reasoning 2: Their litigation against the June 2024 asylum restrictions and their 702 analyses are tailored to U.S. legal standards implicated here. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/aclu-sues-block-biden-asylum-ban-us-mexico-border-2024-06-12/?utm_source=openai))

- Politico
  - Reasoning 1: Well‑established U.S. political news outlet with professional editorial processes; routinely breaks policy news later corroborated elsewhere.
  - Reasoning 2: Reported the administration’s decision to supply antipersonnel landmines to Ukraine, which was then analyzed by rights NGOs; used as a contemporaneous event source. ([politico.com](https://www.politico.com/news/2024/11/20/biden-land-mines-ukraine-00190641?utm_source=openai))

- Axios
  - Reasoning 1: Reputable outlet known for concise, document‑driven reporting and extensive sourcing within U.S. agencies.
  - Reasoning 2: Summarized the State Department’s NSM‑20 report language (credible assurances vs. inability to verify specific incidents) that underpins the Gaza‑arms critique. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2024/05/10/israel-gaza-weapons-broke-law-blinken?utm_source=openai))

- Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official site
  - Reasoning 1: Primary source for rule text and official fact sheets.
  - Reasoning 2: DHS’s own “Circumvention of Lawful Pathways” materials establish the policy features rights groups challenge (e.g., presumptions tied to mode of entry/CBP One). ([dhs.gov](https://www.dhs.gov/news/2023/05/11/fact-sheet-circumvention-lawful-pathways-final-rule?utm_source=openai))

- PEN America / Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)
  - Reasoning 1: Respected press‑freedom organizations; CPJ in particular is widely cited internationally.
  - Reasoning 2: Their statements on the Assange case explain why the prosecution raised system‑level press‑freedom risks relevant to human‑rights analysis. ([cpj.org](https://cpj.org/2024/06/cpj-welcomes-reports-that-assange-will-be-released-in-plea-deal/?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources I considered not trustworthy

- None. I did not rely on or meaningfully consider sources I regard as untrustworthy for this topic. Where possible I used primary sources (ICJ, U.S. government documents) and well‑established NGOs and wire services, and I cross‑checked claims among them.
